meta.methodology:
Read framework.md, torah_170_packages.json, and the full source text torah_170.txt. Reference 170 has zero pre-existing bechina edges in torahData.js. All nodes in both proposed packages are new additions to the dataset for this Torah reference. The additions section identifies every bechina-bearing concept from the source text with its proposed package assignment, source quote, and the explicit language that justifies the bechina classification.

Torah #170 uses three distinct bechina formulas:
(1) 'נִקְרָאִים' (are called) — the strongest explicit bechina formula: naming IS being
(2) 'לְשׁוֹן' (language of / named after) — etymological/phonetic bechina: shared linguistic root reveals shared essential nature. This formula appears throughout Likutay Moharan (e.g., Torah #1 uses 'לְשׁוֹן' equations extensively) and is considered a full bechina in Breslov hermeneutics
(3) 'הַיְנוּ' (namely / that is) — the most explicit equation formula: X, namely Y = X IS Y
(4) Structural parallel usage — the interchangeable use of גּוּף and חֹמֶר in identical syntactic positions ('נִכְנָע גּוּפוֹ' parallel to 'בְּהִכָּנַע הַחֹמֶר') establishes their bechina identity

additions.reason: יִסּוּרִין (afflictions/suffering) is the opening concept of the teaching — 'כָּל אֶחָד לְפִי נִשְׁמָתוֹ וּלְפִי עֲבוֹדָתוֹ, כָּךְ יֵשׁ לוֹ יִסּוּרִים' (each person according to their soul and service has suffering). The bechina equation is explicit: 'כָּל הַיִּסּוּרִין נִקְרָאִים צָרוֹת' — all afflictions ARE CALLED tzarot. יסורין and צרות name the same reality from different angles: יסורין is the experiential term (the subjective experience of being afflicted), while צרות is the structural term (the constriction that produces that experience). They share the essential nature of divinely-sent suffering that both constricts the body and reveals the soul. Polarity 'good' because Torah #170 presents yisurin as positive: they are the mechanism by which spiritual people elevate and carry others.

צָרוֹת (afflictions/troubles; lit. 'constrictions') is the structural term that the teaching elaborates upon most extensively. It is explicitly equated with יסורין via 'נִקְרָאִים' (edge 1) and with צוּרָה via 'לְשׁוֹן' (edge 2). The name itself is the key: 'צָרוֹת' comes from the root צ-ר-ר (to constrict), and the teaching explains they are called צָרוֹת 'עַל שֵׁם שֶׁהֵם מְצֵרִין וּמְעִיקִין לְהַגּוּף' (because they constrict and press on the body). But simultaneously, the word 'צָרָה' is 'לְשׁוֹן צוּרָה' (the language of form/soul) — meaning the very constriction IS the soul-revealing process. This dual etymology (צ-ר-ר = constrict AND צ-ו-ר = form) is the teaching's central linguistic-bechina breakthrough. צרות is the most-connected node in the bechina graph (degree 2: connected to יסורין and to צוּרָה), making it structurally central to the teaching's topology.
additions.source_quote: עַל שֵׁם שֶׁהֵם מְצֵרִין וּמְעִיקִין לְהַגּוּף... נִקְרֵאת צָרָה, לְשׁוֹן צוּרָה

additions.reason: צוּרָה (form; the kabbalistic 'form' as opposed to 'matter') is explicitly identified as the נֶפֶשׁ: 'מְאִירָה הַצּוּרָה, הַיְנוּ הַנֶּפֶשׁ' (the form shines, namely the soul). In Aristotelian-kabbalistic philosophy (which Rebbe Nachman incorporates throughout Likutay Moharan), צוּרָה is the formal/spiritual dimension of reality as opposed to חֹמֶר (matter). The teaching applies this directly: 'בְּהִכָּנַע הַחֹמֶר תִּגְדַּל הַצּוּרָה' (when the matter is subdued, the form grows). This is the classic philosophical dyad applied to soul/body: body = matter/חֹמֶר, soul = form/צוּרָה. The bechina 'צָרָה לְשׁוֹן צוּרָה' links the suffering cluster to this cluster through the linguistic insight that affliction IS form-language. The bechina 'צוּרָה = נֶפֶשׁ' links the form concept to the soul concept. צוּרָה is the pivot/bridge node of the entire teaching, connecting suffering to soul through its double identity as 'that which the tzarah is named after' and 'that which IS the nefesh.' Degree 2 in the bechina graph.
additions.bechina_formula: הַיְנוּ (namely / that is — the strongest equation formula)

additions.reason: נֶפֶשׁ (soul) is the teaching's goal-concept and the climactic revelation: 'הַיְנוּ הַנֶּפֶשׁ' (that is, the soul) — the Rebbe explicitly declares that the צוּרָה he has been discussing IS the נֶפֶשׁ. The teaching's conclusion is built around the soul's capacity: 'הַנֶּפֶשׁ אֶפְשָׁר לָהּ לָשֵׂאת עָלֶיהָ כַּמָּה וְכַמָּה אֲנָשִׁים' (the soul is capable of bearing upon itself many and many people). This is the answer to the question posed in the teaching: the body cannot carry people, but when suffering subdues the body and the soul shines, the soul — as form, not matter — can carry unlimited people to their spiritual root. The נֶפֶשׁ is the dominant node of Package 1: it is the ultimate subject of the teaching, the entity whose capacity is unlimited, and the concept around which the entire argument resolves. The Zohar proof-text ('גּוּפָא דְּלָא סָלֵק בֵּהּ נְהוֹרָא דְּנִשְׁמְתָא' — a body that cannot receive the soul's light) reinforces the centrality of the soul/light as the positive force the teaching is elevating.
additions.source_quote: הַנֶּפֶשׁ אֶפְשָׁר לָהּ לָשֵׂאת עָלֶיהָ כַּמָּה וְכַמָּה אֲנָשִׁים
additions.bechina_formula: הַיְנוּ (namely — equation in reverse direction confirms symmetry)

additions.reason: גּוּף (body) is the physical container that is constricted and subdued by suffering. The teaching frames the body as neutral material: 'אֵיךְ אֶפְשָׁר לַחֹמֶר לִשָּׂא עָלָיו' (how can the material/body carry so many people?) — implying that the body is inherently limited in capacity. When suffering subdues it, it gets out of the way of the soul. The Zohar proof-text uses the metaphor of wood (אָעָא) that must be struck to catch fire — the body is the wood, neutral material that either blocks or conveys the soul's fire. In the context of Torah #170, the body is not evil (it is not associated with the sitra achra or yetzer hara) but is simply the material dimension whose limitation is overcome when subdued by suffering. Polarity: neutral. The bechina 'גּוּף = חֹמֶר' is established by structural parallel usage: wherever the teaching says גּוּף, it means the same thing as where it says חֹמֶר — both names for the physical/material dimension of human existence.
additions.source_quote: נִכְנָע גּוּפוֹ... בְּהִכָּנַע הַחֹמֶר תִּגְדַּל הַצּוּרָה
additions.bechina_formula: structural parallel usage (interchangeable synonyms in identical syntactic contexts)

additions.reason: חֹמֶר (matter/material) is the philosophical term for the physical dimension — the Aristotelian/kabbalistic concept of 'hyle' or prime matter that receives the form (צוּרָה). The teaching explicitly states 'בְּהִכָּנַע הַחֹמֶר תִּגְדַּל הַצּוּרָה' — when the matter is subdued, the form grows. This is the kabbalistic formulation of the body/soul dyad: חֹמֶר (matter, body) and צוּרָה (form, soul) are the two poles of human existence. The Rebbe asks 'אֵיךְ אֶפְשָׁר לַחֹמֶר לִשָּׂא עָלָיו' (how can matter carry so many people?) — meaning the material body is by nature incapable of spiritual lifting; only when matter is subdued and the soul/form takes over does the capacity for spiritual bearing become unlimited. חֹמֶר is the kabbalistic/philosophical register while גּוּף is the more everyday register — they name the same reality from different vocabularies. Neutral polarity: the material is not evil, just limited; it is the neutral substrate that can either block or allow the spiritual.
additions.source_quote: אֵיךְ אֶפְשָׁר לַחֹמֶר לִשָּׂא עָלָיו כָּל כָּךְ אֲנָשִׁים... בְּהִכָּנַע הַחֹמֶר תִּגְדַּל הַצּוּרָה
additions.bechina_formula: structural parallel usage (philosophical synonym of גּוּף in the same teaching context)

concepts_examined_and_excluded.reason: The teaching opens with 'לְפִי נִשְׁמָתוֹ' (according to his neshama). However, this is used in a general introductory sense ('according to one's spiritual level') and is not equated with any other concept through bechina language. The neshama here is a quantifier/qualifier, not a conceptual node being developed. The teaching's primary soul-concept is נֶפֶשׁ (which it does explicitly equate with צוּרָה). Excluded from packages; would require a separate bechina statement to be included.

The act of 'carrying' people (נוֹשֵׂא עֲלָיו הָאֲנָשִׁים) is the eitza-outcome of the entire process: soul shines → soul carries people. This is the causal result, not a bechina-equivalent of any other concept. Excluded from packages. Would appear as an eitza edge: נֶפֶשׁ → נוֹשֵׂא.

The Zohar citation uses 'נְהוֹרָא דְּנִשְׁמְתָא' (light of the soul). However, this is a metaphor within a quoted proof-text (the Zohar), not a primary bechina equation stated by the Rebbe himself in the body of the teaching. The light of the soul (נהורא) is the soul's illuminated state, not a separate concept being equated. Excluded; if the Zohar metaphor were the focus of the teaching it would warrant a bechina node, but here it is supporting evidence for the body/soul dynamic already captured by גּוּף/חֹמֶר and נֶפֶשׁ/צוּרָה.

analysis_notes.note_on_bechina_language: Torah #170 uses three distinct bechina formulas: (1) 'נִקְרָאִים' (are called) for יסורין = צרות; (2) 'לְשׁוֹן' (language of) for צָרָה = צוּרָה — the etymological/phonetic bechina that is the teaching's central innovation; (3) 'הַיְנוּ' (namely) for צוּרָה = נֶפֶשׁ. Additionally, the structural parallel usage of גּוּף and חֹמֶר in identical syntactic contexts establishes a fourth implicit bechina. All four bechina formulas are standard in Likutay Moharan. The 'לְשׁוֹן' formula is particularly significant: it grounds a metaphysical identity (affliction shares the nature of soul-form) in Hebrew linguistics, demonstrating that the language itself encodes the teaching's insight.
analysis_notes.note_on_teaching_argument: Torah #170 makes a striking interpretive move on Psalms 3:2. The psalmist laments 'Lord, how many are my oppressors — many rise against me.' The Rebbe reads this not as complaint but as spiritual statement: 'the more my tzarot multiply (רַבּוּ צָרַי), the more I carry and elevate many (רַבִּים) to their root.' The suffering (צרות) becomes the mechanism of spiritual leadership and elevation. This inversion (oppression → elevation) is made possible by the bechina chain: tzarot = tzurah (soul-form) = nefesh. The soul's unlimited capacity to bear others depends on the body first being subdued by suffering. The teaching thus provides a mystical justification for why spiritual leaders (and anyone operating at a high spiritual level) suffer more as they rise: their greater suffering enables greater soul-capacity and greater ability to carry others.
